source: Langley (1981) Data-driven discovery of physical laws (BACON.1-BACON.3)
finding: BACON is a rule-based program that finds laws in numeric data. It looks for constant values and for linear, product or ratio relations between variables, then makes the new term a variable and repeats.
numbers: Rediscovered Boyle's gas law, Galileo's law of falling bodies, Ohm's law and Kepler's third law from tabulated data (recalled from memory; not opened).
limits: Not opened: the publisher page returned HTTP 403. Details are recalled, not verified this session. Data were clean and one variable was varied at a time.
agent_relevance: Discovery as a small code-run search over terms with a fit check and no model judgment. This matches open mode with a running check.

source: Langley, Simon, Bradshaw, Zytkow (1987) Scientific Discovery: Computational Explorations of the Creative Processes
finding: Book that collects BACON.1-6, GLAUBER, STAHL, DALTON and others. Claim: discovery is ordinary problem solving by heuristic search, so it can be programmed.
numbers: BACON.4 handled intrinsic properties such as specific heat; later versions used symmetry and conservation (recalled; not opened).
limits: Not opened. Systems were run on historical data that had already been cleaned; critics later raised this.
agent_relevance: The frame 'discovery = search with heuristics' is the same as our schema: code-run moves, a fit test, a stop rule.

source: Falkenhainer and Michalski (1986) Integrating quantitative and qualitative discovery: the ABACUS system
finding: ABACUS extended BACON-style discovery by mixing numeric fitting with conditions that mark when a law applies.
numbers: No figures recorded (not opened).
limits: Not opened; cited from memory only.
agent_relevance: Laws have scope conditions. Our agent should record where a found rule holds and where it does not.

source: Udrescu and Tegmark (2020) AI Feynman: a physics-inspired method for symbolic regression
finding: Recursive symbolic regression that uses a neural net to detect symmetry, separability and compositionality, then splits the problem.
numbers: Solved all 100 equations from the Feynman Lectures; the best earlier public software solved 71. On a harder physics test set, success rose from 15% to 90%.
quote: it discovers all of them, while previous publicly available software cracks only 71
limits: Equations are short physics laws with clean data. The set is public, so memory by LLMs is a later worry (see LLM-SRBench).
agent_relevance: The gain comes from checking a structural property by running a fit, then shrinking the search. A cheap code check shrinks the hypothesis space.

source: Udrescu and Tegmark (2020) AI Feynman: what made it work
finding: Its gains come from structure tests (low-order polynomial, symmetry, separability) done before search, not from a bigger search.
numbers: Tests: polynomial fit, translational and rotational symmetry, separability; 100 of 100 equations solved vs 71 for prior public software.
limits: Real data are messier than the clean tables used here.
agent_relevance: Add cheap structural checks that code can run before generation, as an operator.

source: Shojaee et al. (2024) LLM-SR: scientific equation discovery via programming with LLMs
finding: An LLM writes equation skeletons as code, a data optimizer fits the constants, and the best programs go back into the prompt in an evolutionary loop.
numbers: With GPT-3.5 and Mixtral and about 2.5K iterations, it beat symbolic-regression baselines that ran 2M+ iterations. On E. coli growth, out-of-domain NMSE 0.0037 vs above 1 for others.
limits: A small set of physics and biology problems; baselines had no domain text.
agent_relevance: Model proposes, code fits, held-out data judges. That is open mode with a running check (G2, G3).

source: Shojaee et al. (2024) LLM-SR ablations
finding: Removing parts of the loop hurts. Dropping the iterative refinement loop hurt most. Dropping the natural-language problem description also hurt. Letting the LLM write the constants too hurt.
numbers: Without iterative refinement: NMSE 1.01e-1 in-domain, 1.81e-1 out-of-domain. Without skeleton plus optimizer: 3.78e-1 in-domain, 3.75e-1 OOD. Without program form (one-line expressions): worse but milder.
limits: Ablations on the same benchmark set; no significance tests.
agent_relevance: Let code fit numbers and let the model propose structure only. Keep the feedback loop.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench
finding: New benchmark: LSR-Transform (Feynman equations rewritten in other forms) and LSR-Synth (invented equations). Built to block memorization.
numbers: Best system solved only 31.5% of LSR-Transform and 28.1% of LSR-Synth (symbolic accuracy). Llama-3.1-8B error on plain Feynman problems dropped sharply, which the authors read as memorization.
quote: sharp drops in numeric error curves ... suggest memorization rather than gradual discovery
limits: Symbolic accuracy is partly judged by an LLM; domains are physics, chemistry, biology and materials.
agent_relevance: Success on famous laws may be recall. Test open mode on transformed or invented tasks, and check that the answer was not just remembered (G3).

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist
finding: End-to-end system: generate idea, check novelty with Semantic Scholar, write code, run experiments, write paper, review it.
numbers: Cost under $15 per paper. Each review costs $0.25 to $0.50.
limits: Only three ML templates (2D diffusion, NanoGPT, grokking); code starts from a template.
agent_relevance: The full open-mode loop exists and is cheap, but see the failure lines below.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: automated reviewer
finding: A GPT-4o reviewer was tested on ICLR 2022 papers. Reflexion and one-shot each added about 2 points of accuracy. Ensembling did not raise accuracy but cut variance.
numbers: Balanced accuracy 0.65 vs human 0.66; false negative rate 0.39 vs 0.52; false positive rate 0.31 vs 0.17. Correlation with mean human score 0.18 vs 0.14 between two humans. Sonnet 3.5 needed a threshold of 8 because of over-optimism.
limits: ICLR 2022 may be in training data. Accepted papers are camera-ready while rejected ones are submissions, which leaks a signal.
agent_relevance: A model judge is near human level on noisy peer review but over-optimistic. It should not be the final selector (G8).

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: paper yield by model
finding: Across four models on the diffusion template, many ideas fell out before a paper. Mean automated review score was about 3.2 to 3.8 on a 2 to 6 scale.
numbers: Sonnet 3.5: 51 ideas, 49 novel, 38 passed experiments, 38 papers, mean 3.82, max 6.0, about $250. GPT-4o: 51 ideas, 41 novel, 16 papers, mean 3.70, about $300. Cheap model rows: mean 3.2 to 3.3 at $10.
limits: Scores come from the system's own automated reviewer, not human review.
agent_relevance: Even the best run was under the accept bar on average. Cost to completion is a real cut; count it (G7).

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: failure modes
finding: Authors list failures: ideas are very similar across runs and models, many ideas are not implemented, code can be wrong without being noticed, LaTeX fails to compile.
numbers: No single figure; Tables 3 to 5 show a large share of ideas dropped at the experiment stage.
quote: may incorrectly implement an idea, which can be difficult to catch
limits: Self-reported by the system's authors.
agent_relevance: Wrong implementations that look fine need an adversarial code check. Supports G2 and G3.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: novelty check
finding: The system flags an idea as novel after searching Semantic Scholar. Its self-scores for interestingness, novelty and feasibility run too high.
numbers: Of 51 diffusion ideas, 49 flagged novel with Sonnet 3.5 and 41 with GPT-4o.
limits: The flag depends on search coverage and on the model's reading of results.
agent_relevance: A search-based check beats a self-score but is still not a run. Keep the check outside the generating model (G8).

source: Yamada et al. (2025) The AI Scientist-v2
finding: Drops the fixed code template and uses agentic tree search with a vision-model figure checker. Three fully AI papers were sent to an ICLR workshop.
numbers: One paper scored 6.33 average (6, 6, 7), about top 45%, above the workshop bar. The other two were rejected. The accepted paper reported a negative result and was withdrawn after acceptance.
limits: N = 3 papers, one workshop. Authors say it would not pass a main conference (20 to 30% acceptance).
agent_relevance: One success in three is thin. Tree search with a running check is the structure we want.

source: Yamada et al. (2025) AI Scientist-v2: caveats
finding: The authors say the accepted paper has weak justification, possible dataset overlap and wrong captions, and cites loosely.
numbers: 1 of 3 accepted; main-conference acceptance 20 to 30%.
limits: Self-assessment by the same authors.
agent_relevance: Papers can pass review with errors the model did not see: add independent checks.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study
finding: Blind review of LLM ideas against ideas from experts on NLP prompting topics. LLM ideas were rated more novel and slightly less feasible.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition, 79 reviewers, 298 reviews. Novelty mean: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI plus human rerank 5.81 (p < 0.05). Feasibility: human 6.53, AI 6.30, AI rerank 6.41 (not significant). Overall: human 4.56, AI 5.18, rerank 5.45.
limits: Ideas only, not executed projects. Novelty is a human rating. Topics limited to prompting research.
agent_relevance: Models make ideas that read as new. Whether they work is another question; G8 says novelty needs running.

source: Si et al. (2024) Diversity wall and LLM judges
finding: Scaling up generation hits a wall of repeats, and LLM judges rank ideas near chance.
numbers: Of 4000 seed ideas, only about 200 were non-duplicates (cosine similarity above 0.8 counts as duplicate). Judge accuracy on top vs bottom 25% of ideas: GPT-4o direct 50.0, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7, pairwise 53.3, authors' pairwise ranker 56.1.
limits: Small set; chance is 50.
agent_relevance: Sampling more from one model gives repeats (G4). Model judges rank ideas near chance (G5, G8).

source: Yang et al. (2024) Large language models for automated open-domain scientific hypotheses discovery (MOOSE)
finding: Multi-module framework for social-science hypotheses from raw web text, with three feedback loops: present, past and future feedback.
numbers: Test set of 50 recent social-science papers. GPT-4 rating, novelty column: baseline 2.483, MOOSE-base 3.081, with future and past feedback 3.390. Expert rating, same column: 2.276, 2.855, 3.197.
limits: Only 50 papers; GPT-4 and few experts as raters; I read the second column as novelty from the table layout.
agent_relevance: Feedback loops raised rated novelty without any run. That is weaker than a running check.

source: Yang et al. (2025) MOOSE-Chem: rediscovering unseen chemistry hypotheses
finding: Splits discovery into retrieve inspirations, compose a hypothesis, rank. Tested on 51 chemistry papers published after Jan 2024, so the model could not have seen them.
numbers: Inspiration retrieval hit ratio at corpus 1000 to 3000: top 20% of corpus 96.4% and 95.8%; top 4% 88.9% and 86.9%; top 0.8% 69.0% and 70.6%; top 0.016% 46.7% and 52.0%. With screening window 10, 1 round 98.0%, 4 rounds 56.5%; window 60, 1 round 71.6%.
limits: Matched Score is judged by GPT-4o; expert agreement is in an appendix. Only 51 papers.
agent_relevance: Retrieving the right inspiration works well; the combine and rank steps are the weaker links.

source: Yang et al. (2025) MOOSE-Chem: matched score counts
finding: Generated hypotheses often matched the core of the true hypothesis. A background survey helped a little.
numbers: Top Matched Score (GPT-4o), counts of 51 papers at score 5,4,3,2,1,0: with survey 2, 9, 18, 17, 5, 0; without survey 1, 7, 17, 19, 7, 0 (read from garbled PDF text).
limits: Table layout was garbled in extraction; counts may be shifted by a column.
agent_relevance: The pool holds a good hypothesis more often than the top pick does. Test ranking by code over a pool.

source: Qi et al. (2023) Large language models are zero shot hypothesis proposers
finding: Biomedical hypothesis dataset split by date into seen and unseen. LLMs given background could propose hypotheses on unseen literature. Few-shot examples raised verifiability but lowered novelty.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo unseen, zero-shot: novelty 1.42, average 1.90. 5-shot with similar examples: novelty 1.02, verifiability 2.36, average 1.96. Llama-2-70b-chat 5-shot: novelty 1.95, average 2.20.
limits: Scores from an LLM rater on a small numeric scale; BLEU and ROUGE only about 8 to 27.
agent_relevance: Near examples trade novelty for validity. Open mode should not stuff in close examples.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld
finding: Virtual world with 120 tasks across topics and three difficulty levels; scores for task completion, procedure, and discovered explanatory knowledge.
numbers: Human scientists (up to 11): 66% completion, 55% knowledge. Best agent (ReAct) finished 38% of easy and 18% of challenge tasks. Hypothesizer found 34% of gold knowledge on easy and 8% on challenge. Agents scored 60%+ on unit-test sub-skills.
limits: Simulated, not real labs; baseline agents use GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Agents do single steps well and fail at end-to-end discovery. A scaffold must carry hypothesis state across steps.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld agent designs
finding: Three baselines: ReAct, Plan+Execute, Hypothesizer (keeps a list of hypotheses and tests them). Hypothesizer had the best knowledge scores on many tasks.
numbers: Average knowledge score, easy: ReAct 0.25, Plan+Execute 0.11, Hypothesizer 0.34 (as read from the table). Challenge: 0.10, 0.01, 0.08.
limits: Gaps are small, 5 seeds per task, table text partly garbled.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis list kept by program state helps knowledge found, but not by much.

source: Chen et al. (2024) ScienceAgentBench
finding: 102 tasks from 44 peer-reviewed papers in four fields; agents write code to finish data-driven science tasks.
numbers: Best agent solved 32.4% alone and 34.3% with expert knowledge (3 attempts). o1-preview with self-debug: 42.2% at over 10 times the cost. Claude 3.5 Sonnet with self-debug beat OpenHands CodeAct by 10.8% at 17 times lower cost.
limits: Data analysis tasks, not open hypothesis finding; graded by outputs and rubrics.
agent_relevance: Simple self-debug on real output beat a heavier agent at lower cost. Supports G2 and G7.

source: Cross-reading of Si 2024 and Lu 2024
finding: Both papers show the same weakness: models write ideas that sound new, but repeat themselves and are judged near chance by model judges.
numbers: Si: 4000 ideas to about 200 distinct. Lu: ideas similar across runs and models.
limits: Different tasks; both ML or NLP topics.
agent_relevance: Use code-based dedup by embedding distance and a run-based test, not a model's rating of its own ideas.

source: Cross-reading of LLM-SR and LLM-SRBench
finding: LLM-SR reports big gains over symbolic regression on known problems. LLM-SRBench shows that on transformed or invented problems the best score is about 30%.
numbers: Best system 31.5% (Transform) and 28.1% (Synth).
limits: Different test sets and metrics (NMSE vs symbolic accuracy).
agent_relevance: Gains from prior knowledge are real but partly recall. Test open mode on problems the model could not have seen.
